Trinka’s final day comes on his 65th birthday. He first went to work at the hotel in 1963, joining the staff as a teenager. For four decades, he stood at the famous hotel’s Fifth Avenue entrance. Several years ago, during renovations and the Plaza’s partial conversion into condominiums, he moved to the entrance on Central Park South.

Over time, the outgoing Trinka became as familiar a sight along Central Park South as the horse-drawn carriages waiting along the park’s southern edge. Marla Maples, the former wife of Donald Trump, who once owned the Plaza, often gave Trinka a kiss on the cheek when she saw him. Trinka also says he keeps an autographed photograph of Richard Nixon at home, a thank-you gift from the former president that he displays proudly.

Trinka says his many years at the entrance to a place associated with glamour and history have been deeply rewarding. “I never had a bad day in all the years,” he said. Even so, after so much time at the hotel, he decided the moment had come to “bow out gracefully.”

As he leaves the job, Trinka says he will miss having a front-row view of Central Park and seeing the hotel’s guests and residents, whom he calls the “greatest people in the world.” He admits he will also miss “the women.”

Those who live in the building are reluctant to see him go. Resident Joan Spain described him as “a gentleman, refined,” adding, “you don’t find these people anymore.”

His successor, Jimmy O’Connell, understands the challenge of following him. O’Connell said he would consider it enough if he “could be half the doorman” Trinka has been.

The Plaza plans to send Trinka off Thursday afternoon in the lavish style associated with the hotel. Following a champagne farewell in the landmarked Oak Room, management will give him the chance to experience the Plaza the way so many guests he welcomed did: with a complimentary stay at the hotel.

Along with a wealth of celebrity stories, Trinka gained something else during his Plaza career — a different name. Years ago, the hotel issued him a name tag that incorrectly said Edward, although his full name is Edwin. Rather than correcting the mistake, he accepted it, allowed people to call him Edward and even named his son Edward.

**New York** — For nearly half a century, Ed Trinka has stood at one of the most recognizable entrances in New York City, greeting guests beneath the green awning of The Plaza Hotel with a steady smile, a crisp uniform and the kind of memory that made visitors feel as if they were coming home.

On his 65th birthday, Trinka — the hotel’s longest-serving doorman — is retiring after 46 years on the job.

“I’ve opened a lot of doors,” Trinka said, “but what I’ll remember most are the people who walked through them.”

Trinka began working at The Plaza as a young man, long before smartphones, ride-share apps and rolling suitcases changed the rhythm of hotel life. Back then, taxis lined up along Fifth Avenue, guests arrived with steamer trunks and handwritten notes, and a doorman’s job required not only strength and stamina but discretion, warmth and an eye for detail.

Over the decades, Trinka became part of the hotel’s identity — a familiar face for generations of guests, employees and New Yorkers passing by the landmark at the corner of Fifth Avenue and Central Park South.

He welcomed honeymooners who returned years later with children, then grandchildren. He helped first-time visitors navigate the city. He offered directions, hailed cabs in downpours and blizzards, remembered names, celebrated milestones and stood watch as the city transformed around him.

The Plaza, opened in 1907, has long been a symbol of New York glamour, hosting world leaders, celebrities, families and tourists drawn by its history. But for many who came through its doors, Trinka represented something more personal: continuity.

Colleagues describe him as dependable, gracious and quietly funny — the kind of person who could calm a flustered traveler, charm a child and make a weary guest feel instantly cared for.

“He treated everyone like they mattered,” one longtime coworker said. “That’s what made him special. It didn’t matter if you were famous or visiting New York for the first time — Ed made you feel welcome.”

Being a doorman at The Plaza meant witnessing the city’s highs and lows from a front-row seat. Trinka worked through blackouts, parades, snowstorms, economic booms and downturns, and moments when New York itself seemed to pause. Through it all, he returned to his post.

There were famous faces, of course, though Trinka is careful with stories. A good doorman, he says, knows when to speak and when to simply nod.

“You learn to read people,” he said. “Some want to talk. Some just need help with a bag. Some are having the best day of their lives, and some are having a hard one. Your job is to be there.”

On his final day, hotel staff gathered to celebrate him with applause, handshakes and hugs. Guests stopped to offer thanks. Some posed for photos. Others simply wanted one last greeting from the man who had become, for them, part of The Plaza itself.

For Trinka, retiring on his 65th birthday felt fitting — a milestone marked not by fanfare, but by gratitude.

“I’ve been lucky,” he said. “Lucky to have a job I loved, lucky to work with good people and lucky to meet people from all over the world.”

As he steps away from the revolving doors and the steady hum of Fifth Avenue, Trinka said he is looking forward to slower mornings, more time with family and the simple pleasure of being on the other side of the welcome.

But at The Plaza, his absence will be felt.

After 46 years, Ed Trinka is leaving the door. The impression he made on those who passed through it will remain.

---

# The Mayor of 59th Street Takes His Final Bow  
### After four decades at The Plaza, a beloved doorman retires — leaving behind a New York corner that may never feel quite the same.

By [Reporter Name]  
New York

On his last morning at The Plaza Hotel, Vincent “Vinnie” Caruso arrived before sunrise, the way he had for 41 years.

He stepped out of the subway in a navy overcoat, crossed Fifth Avenue as the first taxis rolled past Central Park, and paused beneath the hotel’s green awning, where the gold letters still seemed to glow even in the gray winter light. For decades, this corner — 59th Street and Fifth Avenue — had been his stage, his office, his neighborhood, and, to many who passed through it, his kingdom.

“Morning, Mr. Caruso,” called a bellman, holding the door.

Vinnie smiled.

“Not Mr. Caruso,” he said. “Just Vinnie.”

By noon, that would be impossible. Word had spread quietly among residents, staff, former guests, shopkeepers, chauffeurs, dog walkers, and a few famous faces who had once slipped through The Plaza’s revolving doors under Vinnie’s watchful eye. The man long nicknamed the “mayor of 59th Street” was retiring.

For the city, it was another change on a corner famous for them. For The Plaza, it was the end of an era.

“He knew everyone, and somehow everyone felt like he was waiting just for them,” said Eleanor Whitman, a longtime resident of the hotel’s private residences. “In New York, that is no small gift.”

Caruso, 67, began working at The Plaza in 1983, back when handwritten luggage tags were common, limousines lined the curb three deep, and celebrities still tried, with varying degrees of success, to enter unnoticed. He was 26 then, the son of a Queens transit worker and a seamstress, newly married, and proud of the brass buttons on his uniform.

“I thought I’d do it a year,” he said, laughing. “Maybe two. Then I blinked, and my kids were grown.”

Over four decades, he learned the rhythms of a hotel that has long served as both landmark and living room — a place where wedding parties sweep through in clouds of satin, children press their noses to the Eloise portraits, and tourists look up at the chandeliers as if they have accidentally walked into a movie.

Vinnie’s job, officially, was to open doors, hail taxis, manage arrivals, carry umbrellas, remember names, and keep the sidewalk moving.

Unofficially, it was to make New York feel gracious.

“He had this way of slowing the city down for you,” said Martin Alvarez, who has lived nearby for 22 years and walks past The Plaza each morning with his terrier, Gus. “You could be late, irritated, freezing, whatever. Vinnie would tip his cap and say, ‘Beautiful day if you squint,’ and suddenly you’d laugh. That was his talent.”

There are stories, of course. A good doorman at a grand hotel collects them like matchbooks.

There was the Oscar-winning actress who arrived incognito in oversized sunglasses, only to have Vinnie quietly redirect a waiting crowd of photographers by saying, “Folks, the action’s around the corner,” giving her enough time to slip inside.

There was the rock star who forgot which entrance he had used and ended up chatting with Vinnie for 20 minutes about Italian bakeries in Astoria.

There was the visiting prince whose security team wanted the whole sidewalk cleared until Vinnie gently informed them, “This is Fifth Avenue, gentlemen. Nobody clears Fifth Avenue.”

And there was the famous comedian — Vinnie still refuses to name him — who once asked whether the hotel kept a secret tunnel to Central Park.

“I told him, ‘Sir, if we had one, I’d be charging admission,’” Vinnie said.

His discretion became part of his legend. He never carried a camera. He never asked for autographs. He never repeated what was said in the driveway.

“Celebrities trusted him because he treated them like regular people,” said Denise Park, a former concierge who worked with Caruso for 18 years. “And regular people loved him because he treated them like celebrities.”

That may explain why, on Tuesday afternoon, a small crowd formed beneath the awning despite the cold. Staff members came out in waves. Residents descended from upstairs. A florist from across the avenue brought white roses. A carriage driver raised his whip in salute. Someone produced a sheet cake decorated with a tiny fondant taxi.

A handwritten sign near the entrance read: “Thank you, Mayor Vinnie.”

For some, the nickname began as a joke. Caruso knew the newsstand man, the doormen up and down the block, the Central Park vendors, the NYPD officers posted during parades, the drivers who could be trusted, the ones who could not, and exactly which guests preferred conversation and which preferred silence.

But over time, “mayor” seemed less like a nickname than a job description.

“He kept track of births, graduations, illnesses, anniversaries,” said Barbara Klein, whose family has maintained an apartment in the building for more than a decade. “When my husband died, Vinnie was the first person I saw when I came home from the hospital. He didn’t say anything grand. He just opened the door and said, ‘We’ve got you.’ I’ll never forget that.”

Caruso said he has forgotten plenty: room numbers, flight times, restaurant names, even, once, where he had placed his own gloves. But names stayed with him.

“You remember what matters,” he said. “People want to be seen. That’s the whole trick.”

His final shift was filled with small ceremonies. A family from London who had visited every December for 15 years sent a video message. A Broadway actor stopped by between rehearsals and hugged him hard. A retired executive pressed an envelope into his hand and whispered, “You made this place home.”

At 3 p.m., the hotel’s general manager presented Caruso with a framed photograph of The Plaza entrance taken during a snowstorm in the 1990s. In the corner of the image, barely visible beneath the awning, stood a younger Vinnie, one arm raised to hail a cab.

“I still remember that day,” Caruso said, studying the picture. “Couldn’t feel my toes.”

When asked what he will do next, he offered the practical answer first: spend time with his wife, Linda; visit his grandchildren in New Jersey; sleep past 5 a.m.; maybe take a trip to Sicily.

Then he looked out toward the park, where the bare trees shifted in the wind.

“I’ll miss the corner,” he said. “You get used to being part of the weather.”

By 5 p.m., the sky had darkened and rush-hour traffic had begun its impatient crawl along 59th Street. Caruso changed out of his uniform in the staff locker room, placing his cap carefully in a bag. When he returned to the lobby, the applause began before he reached the door.

For once, the man who had spent a lifetime greeting arrivals seemed unsure how to make an exit.

He hugged the bellmen. He shook hands with security guards. He kissed residents on both cheeks. Outside, a yellow cab pulled to the curb, its driver leaning out the window.

“Vinnie!” he shouted. “Need a ride?”

Caruso laughed.

“Not today,” he called back. “Today I’m walking.”

And so he did. The mayor of 59th Street stepped out from beneath The Plaza’s awning, turned once to look at the doors he had opened thousands upon thousands of times, and raised his hand in farewell.

Then he crossed Fifth Avenue, disappearing into the city he had spent four decades welcoming home.

**At the Door, a Life in White Gloves and Weather**

*For more than half a century, a luxury hotel doorman has stood between the city and its most famous arrivals — opening cars, keeping secrets, and learning that every guest, even a Beatle, needs to be welcomed home.*

By Staff Writer

NEW YORK — On a cold afternoon when the wind comes knifing down the avenue and the taxis stack up three deep along the curb, the doorman still stands as straight as a lamppost.

His cap is squared. His coat is brushed. His white gloves are immaculate.

“Good afternoon, Mrs. Adler,” he says, opening the door of a black town car before the driver can reach the handle. “Careful now — a little ice by the curb.”

Mrs. Adler, who has lived part-time in the hotel for 30 years and appears to be at least 90, pats his arm.

“You see?” she says. “He remembers everything.”

The doorman smiles but does not answer. Remembering, in his line of work, is both a gift and a discipline. He remembers names, faces, birthdays, favorite newspapers, difficult sons-in-law, preferred restaurants, which guests like conversation and which want silence. He remembers the night Liza Minnelli swept in after a performance, still glowing with stage light. He remembers Richard Nixon’s guarded arrival, all clipped movements and men in dark coats. He remembers Jackie Kennedy Onassis stepping from a car with the quiet efficiency of a woman accustomed to being watched.

And he remembers the Beatles.

“Everyone asks about them,” he says later, with the shrug of a man who has answered the question thousands of times. “They were young. Polite. Smaller than you’d think. The screaming was the main thing. You could feel it through the glass.”

For 56 years, Anthony “Tony” Caruso has worked the front entrance of the Hotel St. Aurelia, a limestone grand dame on the Upper East Side whose revolving doors have spun in diplomats, movie stars, opera singers, oil barons, presidents, princesses, and newlyweds who saved for two years to spend one night in a room with a view of the park.

Caruso, 78, has been there for nearly all of them.

He is not the general manager, though several have come and gone in his tenure. He is not listed in the hotel’s brochures, and his name is not stitched into the towels or etched into the silver. But for generations of guests, he is the St. Aurelia’s first impression and last farewell — the man in the tailored coat who turns arrival into ceremony.

“Tony is the lobby before the lobby,” says Margaret Ellison, the hotel’s current general manager. “People think luxury is marble and chandeliers. It isn’t. Luxury is being recognized. It’s someone saying, ‘Welcome back,’ and meaning it.”

Caruso has been saying it since 1968.

He was 20 then, the son of a Queens bus mechanic and a seamstress, recently home from a brief stint in the Army and unsure what to do next. An uncle knew someone who knew someone at the St. Aurelia. The hotel needed a bellman.

“I thought it would be temporary,” Caruso says. “That’s how they get you.”

He began inside, carrying trunks that seemed large enough to contain dining tables, running messages up to suites, learning the geography of service: the staff elevators, the back staircases, the pantry where a nervous young employee could grab coffee at 5 a.m. before the breakfast rush.

Within two years, he was moved to the door.

“The old captain told me, ‘Out here, you don’t just open the door,’” Caruso recalls. “‘You read the street. You read the guest. You keep the hotel calm.’”

The street, in those years, was not always calm. The late 1960s and 1970s brought protests, blackouts, strikes, crime, and the particular New York tension of money and disorder living side by side. At the St. Aurelia entrance, Caruso learned to identify paparazzi by posture, autograph seekers by their shoes, and trouble by the way it moved too quickly toward the curb.

“Some people think the job is strength,” he says. “It’s mostly judgment.”

Judgment meant knowing when to step forward and when to disappear. It meant helping an elderly guest out of a cab with the same urgency reserved for a head of state. It meant never repeating what was overheard when the famous forgot they were famous and spoke freely under the awning.

Asked for stories, Caruso offers them carefully, as if removing old photographs from a drawer.

The Beatles, he says, arrived amid a frenzy so loud that police horses were brought near the block. The hotel had prepared for chaos, but nothing prepared the staff for the pitch of teenage devotion.

“They came in fast,” he says. “Heads down a little, smiling. One of them — I won’t say which — said, ‘Thanks, mate,’ like I’d done something heroic. All I did was open the door.”

Jackie Kennedy Onassis was different. No frenzy, no commotion if it could be helped. She moved with elegance, but not theatrical elegance. Practical elegance.

“She didn’t waste motion,” Caruso says. “She knew where she was going. She was always gracious. Soft voice. Looked you in the eye.”

Richard Nixon, after his presidency, came with the atmosphere that follows men who have been both powerful and publicly wounded.

“That was a heavy arrival,” Caruso says. “You could feel everyone trying not to stare.”

And Liza Minnelli?

At that, his professional reserve cracks into a grin.

“Liza was sunshine,” he says. “Some people arrive and take the air out of a place. She brought air in.”

There have been hundreds of others, though Caruso declines to name most of them. He has watched actors become legends, legends become frail, and children of famous guests return years later with children of their own. He has greeted Saudi princes with entourages, Broadway dancers with duffel bags, exhausted surgeons, nervous grooms, widows returning alone to rooms once booked for two.

A hotel doorman, he says, sees people at moments of transition. They are arriving or leaving. Celebrating or escaping. Beginning honeymoons, ending marriages, recovering from funerals, heading to award ceremonies, coming back from bad medical news.

“You learn that everybody has weather,” he says. “Some people just have better coats.”

His own coat is part of the St. Aurelia’s visual mythology: navy in winter, lighter blue in spring, brass buttons polished to a dignified gleam. In old photographs lining a staff corridor, Caruso appears again and again, first as a lean young man with dark hair and a serious mouth, then broader, then gray at the temples, then silver. The hotel around him changes in subtle ways: the cars grow sleeker, the hemlines rise and fall, the luggage gains wheels, the photographers trade flashbulbs for digital cameras and then smartphones.

Caruso remains at the curb.

“He’s a landmark,” says Ben Patel, a taxi driver who has been picking up fares at the hotel since the 1980s. “You tell a new driver, ‘Go to the place with Tony out front.’ They know.”

The job has changed. Once, guests arrived with steamer trunks and expected their privacy as a condition of civilization. Now, some arrive filming themselves for social media before they have even tipped the driver. Celebrities who once ducked cameras sometimes summon them. The line between guest and audience has blurred.

Caruso has adapted, though not always enthusiastically.

“Phones changed everything,” he says. “Used to be, if a famous person came in, maybe a picture ran the next day. Now it’s everywhere before they reach the elevator.”

His rule is simple: protect the doorway. Not from ordinary curiosity, necessarily, but from indignity.

“People are allowed to come in with dignity,” he says. “That’s the whole idea.”

Among hotel staff, Caruso is known less for celebrity anecdotes than for small acts of vigilance. He has walked housekeepers to the subway after late shifts. He has slipped cash to young bellmen short on rent, always insisting it was a loan and never asking for repayment. He keeps a drawer of umbrellas for guests who forget theirs and a mental ledger of who is likely to need a chair brought outside while waiting for a car.

On his lunch breaks, he eats simply: soup, coffee, sometimes a sandwich wrapped in wax paper by his wife, Elena, whom he married in 1973. They have two daughters, both teachers, and four grandchildren who find his fame within the hotel amusing.

“They’ll say, ‘Grandpa, are you on TikTok?’” he says. “I tell them, ‘I’m on the sidewalk.’”

Retirement has become a subject others raise more often than he does. His knees ache in damp weather. He no longer works the overnight shift. In winter, a younger doorman quietly checks to make sure he has taken his break.

But Caruso resists the notion that he is performing nostalgia.

“I’m not here because of the old days,” he says. “I’m here because someone is arriving today.”

That afternoon, arrivals come steadily. A family from London emerges from a yellow cab surrounded by luggage and confusion. Caruso directs the bags, welcomes the parents, bends slightly to greet the children.

“First time in New York?” he asks.

The boy nods.

“Well,” Caruso says, swinging the door open with the gravity of a curtain rising, “then we’d better make it a good one.”

A few minutes later, a chauffeured sedan glides up. Caruso recognizes the guest before the car stops. He steps forward, opens the door, and offers his hand — not too much, not too little. The guest smiles with the relief of being expected.

It is a small moment, almost invisible in a city addicted to spectacle. No screaming fans. No flashbulbs. No famous name to drop later. Just a man at a door, doing what he has done for more than half a century: standing between the hard weather of the street and the promise, however temporary, of being welcomed inside.

Asked what makes a great doorman, Caruso thinks for a while.

“Memory,” he says first. Then he reconsiders. “No. Kindness. Memory helps. But kindness is the thing.”

Outside, the wind rises again. Caruso adjusts his gloves, looks toward the next car, and takes his place beneath the awning.
